record_type_quote: This study tested a new longitudinal sample of children (n = 124) from age 24 to 48 months.

targets.title: Which fearful toddlers should we worry about? Context, fear regulation, and anxiety risk.
targets.evidence_quote: The goals of the present study included (1) replication of identifying a pattern of dysregulated fear in toddlers (Buss, 2011) in a new sample; (2) replication of the prediction from toddler dysregulated fear to elevated social inhibition (Buss, 2011; Buss et al., 2013); and (3) extending our understanding of the implications of dysregulated fear for children’s development by linking this pattern of high fearfulness in low-threat contexts to physiological reactivity as a putative psychophysiological marker of dysregulated emotion processes in toddlerhood. Results were largely consistent with expectations—we were able to replicate the identification of children with dysregulated fear in this new sample, showed that this pattern of fear responding predicted inhibition across early childhood, and identified modest evidence for the idea that children who manifest a dysregulated fear pattern of behavior would also show a distinct pattern of physiological responding to laboratory challenges.
targets.outcome_quote: The present study, which replicates and extends our previous work ([blinded for review]), contributes to this literature by demonstrating robustness in this pattern of fear as a marker of risk for anxiety-related problems. We demonstrated, in a second cohort of children, that a dysregulated pattern of fearful behavior - characterized by high fear in low threat situations – is associated with social inhibition across a 2-year period and is also associated with a different pattern of cardiac reactivity.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The stated replication goals explicitly name this original; the overall verdict supports dysregulated fear and its longitudinal association with inhibition. Differences in curve modeling and new RSA analyses do not reverse this verdict.
